sources.subject: Root-vegetable purées
sources.title: Potential of Two Vegetable Plants in Reducing Lead Contamination in Soil
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/lead contamination Root-vegetable purées/10-12911-22998993-151092.pdf
sources.sample_population: Greenhouse Crassocephalum crepidioides and Amaranthus sp.; three blocks, conflicting reported plant counts
sources.intro: Lestari and Rosyidah compared lead accumulation and growth in two vegetable species grown in lead-amended soil and compost in Malang, Indonesia. Lead treatment reduced growth and the reported shoot-to-root translocation factors. The table supports a narrower interpretation than the paper’s broad phytoextraction conclusion: factors exceed one only in the controls.
sources.key_numbers:
The greenhouse experiment ran from April to July 2021. Table 3 (PDF p. 5) reports the following mean translocation factors. Its heading says ppm although the stated calculation is a ratio. C denotes Crassocephalum crepidioides and A denotes Amaranthus sp.; the source treatment labels are preserved.

| Treatment | Reported factor |
| --- | --- |
| C0 | 1.18 |
| C3 | 0.87 |
| C6 | 0.74 |
| A0 | 1.20 |
| A3 | 0.99 |
| A6 | 0.28 |

Tables 1–2 (PDF p. 3) provide all treatment-level height and leaf-area means at 6, 12, 18, 24 and 30 days after transplanting; the batch evidence register retains these 60 auxiliary growth observations separately from metal concentrations.
sources.methods: A randomized block greenhouse experiment used soil and compost mixed 1: 1, with lead added one week before transplanting. The text prints doses of 0.3 and 6 g per polybag, while treatment codes use C 3/A 3 and C 6/A 6. Lead in roots and shoots was measured by atomic absorption spectrophotometry. The paper states three replicate blocks; the abstract says three sample plants per treatment and Methods says five. It describes means with standard errors and Duncan multiple-range testing, but does not supply exact numeric error bars for the figures.
sources.implications: This is experimental remediation and soil-to-plant pathway evidence. It does not characterize unamended market vegetables, quantify field-scale lead removal, or establish the suitability of harvested biomass for food. Increased root retention under treatment must remain distinct from successful removal of lead from soil.
sources.fitness: EF-3; experimental remediation evidence with source-internal inconsistencies. Tables support source-native growth and translocation observations, not ordinary product occurrence or a validated remediation recommendation.
sources.notes:
Table 3 is retained over conflicting prose values of 1.15 and 1.34 and the blanket claim that translocation factors exceed one. The 0.3-versus-3 treatment-dose ambiguity and three-versus-five plant count are unresolved source reporting discrepancies. Figures 1–3 have unlabelled bar heights; exact biomass, chlorophyll, lead concentration and error-bar values cannot be recovered without digitization or author data. No concentration basis or unit was invented for the lead figure. The microscopy-free AAS method does not establish lead speciation.

Matrix vocabulary extension: experimental-plant denotes greenhouse remediation plants; it is not a commercial food-occurrence row.

sources.subject: Root-vegetable purées
sources.title: Wastewater Irrigation and Accumulation of Heavy Metals in Vegetable Crops (Broccoli and Cauliflower)
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/Heavy metals Root-vegetable purées/10-25130-tjas-23-2-13.pdf
sources.sample_population: Broccoli and cauliflower field experiment; three irrigation regimes and three replicate blocks per treatment, 2018–2019
sources.intro: Rahim measured lead, cadmium, iron and copper in dried edible broccoli and cauliflower heads grown under three irrigation regimes in Sulaymaniyah, Iraq. The tables preserve crop-specific differences: wastewater-irrigated broccoli had the largest listed values for the four metals, whereas cauliflower cadmium was greatest under alternating irrigation.
sources.key_numbers:
The experiment used three replicate blocks, with transplanting on 20 September 2018 and harvest on 1 February 2019. Tables 3–4 (PDF pp. 4–5; printed pp. 165–166) report means with an unspecified plus/minus dispersion, all in µg/g of dried edible tissue. B denotes broccoli and C denotes cauliflower; W is wastewater, A alternating irrigation, and the final C clean water.

| Treatment | Pb | Cd | Fe | Cu |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B-W2 | 0.0250 ± 0.0006 | 0.0421 ± 0.0007 | 4.2247 ± 0.0009 | 0.1513 ± 0.0003 |
| B-A2 | 0.0245 ± 0.0003 | 0.0403 ± 0.0003 | 4.2173 ± 0.0003 | 0.1483 ± 0.0003 |
| B-C2 | 0.0241 ± 0.0003 | 0.0387 ± 0.0006 | 4.2117 ± 0.0007 | 0.1437 ± 0.0012 |
| C-W1 | 0.0240 ± 0.0000 | 0.0397 ± 0.0006 | 4.2190 ± 0.0005 | 0.1510 ± 0.0006 |
| C-A1 | 0.0242 ± 0.0003 | 0.0417 ± 0.0003 | 4.2130 ± 0.0015 | 0.1487 ± 0.0003 |
| C-C1 | 0.0239 ± 0.0007 | 0.0383 ± 0.0009 | 4.2077 ± 0.0017 | 0.1447 ± 0.0007 |
sources.methods: The randomized complete block field experiment at the University of Sulaimani compared clean water, Tanjero River wastewater and an alternating clean/wastewater schedule. Edible heads were washed with distilled water, shade-dried, ground and mixed. Nitric and perchloric-acid digestion preceded atomic absorption spectrometry for Pb, Cd, Fe and Cu. XLSTAT and Tukey comparisons were used. No element-specific detection limits, recoveries or reference materials are reported.
sources.implications: The paired treatment summaries contribute source-native vegetable occurrence and irrigation-pathway evidence. The dried basis is not interchangeable with fresh vegetables. The experiment is site- and season-specific and does not characterize all river water, all Iraqi produce or long-term dietary exposure.
sources.fitness: EF-3; directly measured edible-product summaries from a small controlled field experiment, with unreported analytical quality-control details and dispersion type. Summary-only status does not by itself exclude the source from later appropriately scoped analysis.
sources.notes:
Tables retain more precision than the abstract. B-W 2 is interpreted using the Methods and figure legend as wastewater despite prose calling it alternating irrigation. The table gives wastewater SAR 2.74 while prose says 2.24. Several auxiliary soil-unit labels appear erroneous and are retained as printed in the structured record. The source’s claims that values are below WHO/FAO limits and that river water is clean are not independently verified legal or health conclusions. No fresh-weight conversion is made.

Matrix vocabulary extensions vegetables and wastewater distinguish measured crop heads from environmental irrigation solutions.

sources.subject: Root-vegetable purées
sources.title: Effects of sewage water irrigation on heavy metals accumulation in vegetables in peri-urban areas of Faisalabad, Pakistan
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/Occurrence Root-vegetable purées heavy metals/10-54219-arr-03-1-2025-418.pdf
sources.sample_population: Three representative plants per sampled crop/site; spinach at Ghulam Muhammad Abad and cauliflower at Chokera, Faisalabad
sources.intro: Abubakar and colleagues measured seven metals in sewage water, soil, spinach and cauliflower at two peri-urban sites in Faisalabad, Pakistan. The paper reports substantial differences between the two crop/site combinations, but its design does not separate plant-species effects from location. Concentrations are retained with the source’s measurement and tissue limitations.
sources.key_numbers:
Site I is Ghulam Muhammad Abad and Site II is Chokera. Figure 4 identifies three replicates; its caption supplies mg/L for water and mg/kg for soil and vegetables. The numerical means are printed in Results 3.5 (PDF pp. 6–7). The plant-metal method uses dried leaf material.

| Matrix and site | Cd | Co | Pb | Cr | tHg | Cu | Ni |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Site I water | 0.17 | 0.72 | 1.07 | 1.79 | 1.38 | 2.66 | 0.55 |
| Site II water | 0.50 | 0.66 | 0.87 | 1.23 | 1.92 | 3.21 | 0.87 |
| Site I soil | 1.67 | 3.94 | 2.96 | 4.39 | 5.61 | 4.10 | 7.43 |
| Site II soil | 2.36 | 6.09 | 5.39 | 5.85 | 4.64 | 2.93 | 5.56 |
| Site I spinach | 3.58 | 4.71 | 6.13 | 9.43 | 3.83 | 3.11 | 4.77 |
| Site II cauliflower | 3.92 | 5.55 | 7.76 | 5.71 | 1.94 | 2.51 | 2.68 |

The source reports spinach CAT/POD activities of 81/125 and cauliflower activities of 142/60 Units/g fresh weight (Results 3.4). These biochemical endpoints remain separate from metal concentrations.
sources.methods: Water, surface soil and vegetables were collected at the two sewage-irrigated sites. The text describes spinach above-ground material and cauliflower heads with associated leaves, while the metal method specifically digests 0.2 g dried leaves in sulfuric acid and hydrogen peroxide. Vegetables were dried at 60°C for 24 hours for dry-weight analysis. Co, Cd, Cr, Pb, Cu, Ni and Hg were measured with an iCAP-6300 Duo ICP-OES. The source uses ANOVA and an LSD comparison at 5%, with figure error bars described as SD for three replicates. Sampling dates, analytical LODs, recoveries and certified reference materials are not provided.
sources.implications: These are localized paired environmental and crop measurements, with plant results routed as leafy-tissue evidence. They do not establish a cauliflower-head concentration, a fresh-weight concentration, or a causal reduction in biomass from metal exposure. Industrial source attribution is proposed by the authors, rather than measured by a source-apportionment experiment.
sources.fitness: EF-3; source-reported occurrence summaries with crop/site confounding, unresolved cauliflower tissue composition and analytical reporting gaps. Water and soil values remain upstream context.
sources.notes:
Water prose labels mg/kg, but Figure 4 explicitly labels mg/L; the caption governs the water transcription and the conflict is retained. The abstract calls 29.86 NTU electrical conductivity, whereas the Results identify it as turbidity. The text cites Table 1, but no Table 1 is present in the preserved PDF. Exact figure SDs and physiological bar values are not printed numerically. Claims of safe-limit exceedance and biomass reduction are not independently validated; comparing different crops/sites does not demonstrate a treatment effect. Total Cr and Hg do not establish Cr(VI) or methylmercury.

Matrix vocabulary extensions vegetables and wastewater distinguish measured leaves from sewage water; species, site and tissue remain in the structured groups.

sources.subject: Root-vegetable purées
sources.title: Assessment of the Level of Heavy Metals in Irrigation Water, Farm Soil, and Vegetables Grown in Gobbiya Dam, Bogoro Local Government Area Bauchi State, Nigeria
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/Occurrence Root-vegetable purées heavy metals/10-37933-jete-7-4-2025-2568.pdf
sources.publication: Journal of Energy Technology and Environment 7(4):79–92
sources.sample_population: Four vegetable species and associated soil/water at Gobbiya Dam, Bauchi State; n=3 replicate measurements, independent field sample count unspecified
sources.intro: Joseph and colleagues measured seven metals in kenaf, chili pepper, tomato and spinach plant parts, with associated soil and irrigation water from Gobbiya Dam in Nigeria. The paper separates edible leaves or fruits from roots and stems. Its concentration tables are preserved independently of several inconsistent safety comparisons and a soil-index calculation that uses water standards.
sources.key_numbers:
Tables 1–4 (PDF pp. 4–6) report mean ± SD with n=3 replicate measurements. Selected edible parts are shown below in mg/kg of oven-dried material; the structured evidence retains all sampled organs and the repeated soil/water observations once. BDL means below an unreported detection limit.

| Plant part | tAs | Fe | Cd | Cu | Cr | Pb | Ni |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Kenaf leaves | 0.018 ± 0.015 | 0.536 ± 0.076 | 0.064 ± 0.004 | BDL | 0.082 ± 0.017 | 0.051 ± 0.006 | 0.181 ± 0.105 |
| Chili pepper fruits | 0.032 ± 0.004 | 1.358 ± 0.114 | 0.295 ± 0.307 | 0.347 ± 0.036 | 0.078 ± 0.011 | 0.048 ± 0.007 | 0.217 ± 0.083 |
| Tomato fruits | 0.055 ± 0.001 | 0.563 ± 0.050 | 0.084 ± 0.004 | 0.064 ± 0.053 | 0.101 ± 0.010 | 0.043 ± 0.006 | 0.267 ± 0.051 |
| Spinach leaves | 0.025 ± 0.011 | 1.345 ± 0.104 | 0.075 ± 0.002 | 0.242 ± 0.028 | 0.079 ± 0.008 | 0.052 ± 0.004 | 0.298 ± 0.020 |

Tables 5–8 retain organ-specific bioaccumulation factors, leaf/root translocation factors, the source’s contamination-factor calculation, and profile correlations as separate statistical records. They are not additional concentration samples.
sources.methods: Vegetables were washed, oven-dried at 80°C for 24 hours, pulverized and digested with a sulfuric/perchloric/nitric-acid mixture. Soil was collected at 0–20 cm, composited, dried and digested separately. Acid-preserved water was digested with nitric acid. Atomic absorption spectrometry measured As, Fe, Cd, Cu, Cr, Pb and Ni without species separation. The source reports triplicate measurements and SD, ANOVA and a post-hoc comparison, but no instrument-specific LODs, certified-reference results or field sample count.
sources.implications: The organ-resolved dry-weight values support local occurrence and irrigation-pathway analysis. Roots, stems and non-edible leaves are retained as pathway context rather than assigned to edible-product distributions. Broad leafy-vegetable and herb/spice ingredient routes retain kenaf and chili identity in the structured record without substituting a named cultivar.
sources.fitness: EF-3; measured organ-level occurrence summaries with limited sampling and analytical quality documentation. Transfer metrics and correlations are source-model outputs; the soil contamination-factor calculation is methodologically unsuitable for an independent soil-hazard claim.
sources.notes:
The same soil and water means recur in Tables 1–4 and are not treated as four independent samples. The text incorrectly generalizes several BAF results; Table 5 contains lead factors below one and nickel factors below one. Table 7 explicitly divides soil values by WHO water standards, mixing scopes/bases; its contamination labels are not adopted. The paper prints inconsistent arsenic vegetable limits (0.05 in tables and 0.5 below figures) and inconsistent exceedance prose. These secondary regulatory comparisons are not ingested as legal limits. BDL-derived ratio zeros are not measured concentration zeros. Arsenic is total/unspeciated and chromium is not Cr(VI).

Matrix vocabulary extensions vegetables, non-edible-plant-tissue and irrigation-water distinguish edible organs, experimental non-food tissues and sampled dam water. The paper does not identify the sampled dam water as wastewater.

sources.subject: Root-vegetable purées
sources.title: Occurrence and Risk Assessment of Pesticides, Phthalates, and Heavy Metal Residues in Vegetables from Hydroponic and Conventional Cultivation
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/Occurrence Root-vegetable purées heavy metals/10-3390-foods13081151.pdf
sources.sample_population: Shanghai farms, 2022–2023: hydroponic/conventional lettuce 32/26, celery 15/20, tomato 20/22, cucumber 19/23; total 86/91.
sources.intro: Shanghai farm samples had lower reported lead and cadmium concentrations under hydroponic cultivation than conventional soil cultivation. The element-specific summaries combine four vegetables, while commodity-specific means combine lead with cadmium; neither split can be reconstructed into commodity-by-element concentrations from the preserved main paper.
sources.key_numbers:
| System | Element | Mean µg/kg | Median | Maximum | EDI µg/kg BW/day | THQ | Detected % | Paper exceedance % |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| hydroponic | Pb | 4.77 | 3.6 | 13.4 | 0.0192 | 0.00481 | 68.6 | 0 |
| hydroponic | Cd | 0.91 | 0.65 | 5.1 | 0.00367 | 0.00367 | 46.51 | 0 |
| conventional | Pb | 49.1 | 36.4 | 277 | 0.198 | 0.0495 | 79.12 | 1.1 |
| conventional | Cd | 11.5 | 8.48 | 33 | 0.0464 | 0.0464 | 81.32 | 0 |

Commodity-specific **combined Pb+Cd means**, conventional/hydroponic (µg/kg): lettuce 80.6/5.7; celery 51.3/3.2; cucumber 58.6/6.4; tomato 47.9/5.6. Soil Pb/Cd: 13.02 ± 4.89 / 0.13 ± 0.02 mg/kg; hydroponic irrigation water: 0.036 ± 0.012 / 0.00017 ± 0.00008 mg/L (§3.3).
sources.methods: Fresh produce purchased directly from Shanghai farms in 2022–2023, vacuum freeze-dried for analysis. Pb and Cd measured by ICP-MS (Agilent 7500 CX); details refer to an earlier method. Means exclude results below LOQ (§2.5). Exposure model uses 242 g vegetables/day and 60 kg adult body weight. The preserved main PDF does not explicitly reconcile the reported concentration basis with freeze-dried preparation.
sources.implications: Supports a local cultivation-system comparison and the soil/irrigation pathway. It does not establish commodity-specific Pb or Cd distributions or universal hydroponic safety. Mixed-contaminant hazard indices include pesticides and phthalates; their interpretation remains source-reported.
sources.fitness: EF-2 for qualified comparative occurrence; EF-3 for the exposure model. Preserve summary statistics; require commodity-by-element data and basis clarification before narrower row admission.
sources.notes: Novel matrix labels vegetables and irrigation-water identify produce and environmental water separately. No speciation inferred. Tables govern the pooled means; §3.3 fold-change statements do not consistently reproduce its displayed combined means. Figure/text overlap on PDF p 10 is not a second observation. Supplement Table S 6 is referenced but absent from this preserved PDF. Source-reported legal comparisons are not verified regulatory instruments.

observations.note: Four commodities combined; mean excludes <LOQ. Basis not explicitly reconciled after freeze drying. Exposure and exceedance are paper models, not HMI safety findings.

sources.title: Study of Peculiarities of Accumulation of Heavy Metals and Arsenic in Medicinal Plant Raw Materials of Synanthropic Flora of Voronezh Region
sources.file: Root-vegetable purées raw ingredient heavy metals/10-14258-jcprm-20230211725.pdf
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/Root-vegetable purées raw ingredient heavy metals/10-14258-jcprm-20230211725.pdf
sources.sample_population: Ten medicinal plant species/tissues at 51 Voronezh-region territories; July aerial-part and September root collections, 2015–2020; independent sample total not specified.
sources.intro: Dyakova compares nine elements in medicinal plant materials collected in disturbed and control environments in Russia’s Voronezh region during 2015–2020. The reported ranges preserve tissue and environmental setting; the paper also proposes regional background means across species.
sources.methods: Pharmacopoeial medicinal herbs, leaves, flowers and roots collected from 51 sites including three reserve/control areas, agricultural areas, industrial/transport settings and other disturbed locations. Collections in 2015–2020; AAS using MGA-915 MD and Russian pharmacopoeial method OFS.1.2.2.2.0012.15. Concentrations are reported in mg/kg medicinal raw material; moisture basis, sample-specific dates, replicate counts and numeric detection limits are not supplied in the preserved paper.
sources.implications: Supports geographic and tissue-specific contamination evidence for botanical raw materials and environmental attribution hypotheses. It does not measure finished supplements or isolate an individual polluter’s causal contribution.
sources.fitness: EF-2 for species/tissue and disturbed/control ranges; background means are mixed-species context. Basis and sampling-detail gaps remain visible and do not erase reported summaries.
sources.notes:
English byline and citation on PDF p 8 establish Dyakova, publication year 2023 and DOI. The English title is used here; numerical extraction follows Russian Tables 1–2. Novel medicinal-plant-material matrix denotes raw pharmacopoeial herbs, not finished supplements. Zero-valued Hg flower cells are retained as source reporting/censoring evidence, not zero exposure. Total As/Hg/Cr are not inorganic As, methylmercury or Cr(VI). Source pharmacopoeial comparisons are secondary context, not new regulatory-register rows.

Table 2 background means have an internal consistency problem: Cd 0.08 mg/kg exceeds every Table 1 control upper endpoint (maximum 0.04), and Zn 40.23 exceeds every control upper endpoint (maximum 38.1). They remain source-reported inconsistent context, not accepted background estimates.

sources.title: Efficacy Of Aloe Vera Powder in Bioremediation of Heavy Metals from Waste Water
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/Root-vegetable purées powder heavy metals/10-54393-mjz-v3i1-37.pdf
sources.sample_population: Lahore laboratory aloe-powder adsorption solutions; independent sample and replicate totals not stated.
sources.intro: This laboratory paper tests aloe leaf powder for zinc and sodium adsorption. It is retained as remediation literature with serious quantitative limitations: negative zinc concentration estimates and a reported 500% sodium removal invalidate the paper’s efficacy claims as treatment evidence.
sources.key_numbers:
Reported zinc removal: 9.495% at 1.4% aloe, 10.237% at 4% aloe (p 3 prose; Table 3 rounds to 10.24% but labels the metal sodium). Table 2 reports zinc estimates −9.536363636 ppm for both a treated sample and the control, and 7.072727273 ppm at 1.4% aloe. Sodium Table 5 reports **500%**, which cannot represent ordinary removal efficiency. These are preserved as source-error diagnostics, not accepted physical removal results.

Tables 1–5 retain the full pH series, calibration concentrations/responses and sample estimates in structured context records.
sources.methods: Aloe leaves shade-dried for two weeks, heated at 50–60°C and ground; phosphoric-acid pretreatment described. Adsorption at 37°C and 120 rpm, 25–40 minutes. Zn measured by AAS, Na by flame photometry. Dose percentages differ across Methods, tables and prose; wastewater sampling origin and replication are not adequately described.
sources.implications: Documents an attempted biosorption approach and a reproducibility gap. It cannot support validated percentage removal, potable-water safety or aloe-based treatment efficacy. Sodium data are auxiliary diagnostics.
sources.fitness: EF-X for claimed quantitative efficacy because calibration outputs and removal arithmetic are internally inconsistent; retain explicit context-only experimental records.
sources.notes: Novel adsorption-solution matrix identifies laboratory remediation solutions. Sodium is not promoted to a heavy-metal page. Negative estimates and >100% removal are not corrected by inventing replacement values. Table 3 zinc/sodium label conflict is explicit; exact pH is not a proxy for adsorption. No food or supplement concentration was measured.

sources.title: Yield Assessment of Beetroot and Potato, Cultivated on Ordinary Chernozem Contaminated with Heavy Metals
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/Root-vegetable purées extract heavy metals/10-18619-2072-9146-2017-5-74-75.pdf
sources.sample_population: Three-replicate small-plot field experiment in Oktyabrsky district, Rostov region, 2015; beet Bordeaux 237 and potato Udacha.
sources.intro: A 2015 Rostov-region field experiment measured copper, zinc and lead in beetroot and potato grown on artificially metal-amended chernozem. Adding mineral fertilizer reduced several crop concentrations relative to the metal-only treatment, while yield responses differed between crops.
sources.key_numbers:
| Treatment | Cu beet | Cu potato | Zn beet | Zn potato | Pb beet | Pb potato |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| control | 2.5 | 4.7 | 2.7 | 3.6 | 0.4 | 0.3 |
| 100 mg/kg each metal | 5.4 | 5 | 11.2 | 9.6 | 0.7 | 0.6 |
| metals + NPK | 4.5 | 4.7 | 7.2 | 8.4 | 0.4 | 0.5 |

Crop concentrations are mg/kg, with weight basis unspecified. Beet yields control/metals/metals+NPK: 25.4/21.5/22.3 t/ha; potato: 30.0/34.1/38.5 t/ha. Soil total/mobile concentrations and LSD values are preserved separately (Tables 1–3).
sources.methods: Three replicated plots per treatment at Donskoye experimental farm, Rostov region, Russia, 2015; Cu, Zn and Pb acetates added to 30 cm depth at nominal 100 mg/kg each. Total soil metals by XRF; mobile fractions by 1 N ammonium acetate buffer pH 4.8. Plant dry ashing at 450°C, nitric/hydrochloric acid dissolution and AAS; preparation does not establish the reporting moisture basis.
sources.implications: Supports crop-specific agronomic mitigation and soil-to-crop transfer evidence. Artificially amended experimental crops are not a market-occurrence distribution. Paper limit comparisons remain secondary context.
sources.fitness: EF-2 for experimental concentration/yield comparisons, with fertilizer-dose and weight-basis qualifications. No direct finished-food threshold inference.
sources.notes: The Methods and Table 2 label the fertilizer N 60 P 60 K 60; Tables 1 and 3 instead print N 60 P 90 K 60. Preserve treatment as metals+NPK without inventing the phosphorus dose. Novel experimental-crop matrix keeps crop experiments separate from market surveys. Potato Pb 0.5 mg/kg equals the paper’s displayed comparator; blanket “below” wording is not adopted. No regulatory ceiling is created from this paper.

sources.subject: Root-vegetable purées
sources.title: Removal of Heavy Metals from Industrial Sludge Using Soil Washing Technique
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/Root-vegetable purées washing heavy metals/ajw190036.pdf
sources.publication: Asian Journal of Water, Environment and Pollution 16(3):83–89
sources.sample_population: Industrial sludge collected at Doddaballapur, Bangalore, November2013; column-test replication not specified.
sources.intro: Column washing of Bangalore-area industrial sludge removed substantially more metals with hydrochloric acid plus EDTA than with distilled water. This is a remediation experiment relevant to sludge contamination pathways, with no measurements in food or a demonstrated safe land-application endpoint.
sources.key_numbers:
| Metal | Initial mg/kg | Water removal % | HCl+EDTA removal % | Dispersion cm²/s | Retardation factor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cu | 92.3 | 12.3 | 93.7 | 1.5e-05 | 39 |
| Zn | 152.7 | 5.8 | 98.4 | 7.5e-05 | 35 |
| Fe | 414.5 | 0 | 79.3 | 1.1e-05 | 42 |
| Cr | 74.2 | 0 | 71.2 | 6e-06 | 47 |
| Cd | 4.7 | 0 | 94.2 | 0.00011 | 22.5 |
| Ni | 52.3 | 2.3 | 88.7 | 9e-06 | 45 |
| Pb | 11.2 | 0 | 82.8 | 0.0001 | 39 |

Figure 4 labels provide greater precision: Cu 93.74%, Zn 98.44%, Fe 79.32%, Ni 88.74%, Cd 94.17%, Pb 82.84%, Cr 71.17%. These coexist with the rounded prose values above.

The initial sludge mg/kg reporting basis is not stated in the source.
sources.methods: Sludge collected November 2013 and analyzed using USEPA 3050 B. Air-dried, 2 mm-sieved material compacted to 0.98 g/cm³ and 33.5% water content; pore volume 56.55 cm³. Columns compared distilled water against 0.1 N HCl+0.1 N EDTA. Transport parameters fitted to experimental elution curves. Sampling and analytical-replicate counts and numeric detection limits are not provided.
sources.implications: Supports laboratory washing and contaminant-transport comparisons. Metal-rich leachate still requires management; the study does not establish agricultural reuse or field-scale safety.
sources.fitness: EF-2 for source-reported removal and transport estimates; environmental remediation context, with replication and reporting-basis gaps.
sources.notes: Novel industrial-sludge matrix prevents environmental concentrations entering food rows. The prose order puts Pb 82.8 before Ni 88.7; retain numeric values without the incorrect ranking. The prose 70–95% range conflicts with its exact Zn 98.4%; exact element values govern. Curves have no complete tabulated time series; record a data gap rather than inventing chart precision. Cr is unspeciated, not Cr(VI).

sources.subject: Root-vegetable purées
sources.title: Speciation and distribution of chromium (III) in rice root tip and mature zone: The significant impact of root exudation and iron plaque on chromium bioavailability
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/Root-vegetable purées chromium speciation/10-1016-j-jhazmat-2023-130992.pdf
sources.sample_population: Controlled Xiangzaoxian31 rice seedling experiment, three treatment replicates; no rice grain or market samples.
sources.intro: Rice seedlings exposed to trivalent chromium retained chromium in roots and surface iron plaques. Synchrotron speciation distinguished ferrihydrite-bound from organic-associated Cr(III), with different proportions in root tips and mature zones; the study concerns an upstream uptake mechanism rather than grain contamination.
sources.key_numbers:
| Treatment | Compartment | Cr mean±SE mg/kg | Fe mean±SE mg/kg | Cr distribution % | Fe distribution % |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fe80-CK | iron-plaque-DCB | 0 ± 0 | 41.26 ± 2.8 | — | 90.7 |
| Fe80-CK | root | 0 ± 0 | 1.95 ± 0.43 | — | 4.3 |
| Fe80-CK | shoot | 0 ± 0 | 0.4 ± 0.04 | — | 5.0 |
| Fe80-Cr(III) | iron-plaque-DCB | 1.89 ± 0.14 | 62.73 ± 2.6 | 37.3 | 88.7 |
| Fe80-Cr(III) | root | 2.66 ± 0.14 | 3.87 ± 0.65 | 53 | 5.3 |
| Fe80-Cr(III) | shoot | 0.04 ± 0 | 0.34 ± 0.01 | 9.7 | 6 |

Figure 4 c ferrihydrite-bound/organic-associated Cr(III): root-tip spot 2 42/58%, tip spot 1 36/64%, mature spot 2 87/13%, mature spot 1 83/17%. Table 2 isotope results and Table 1 LSD values are preserved separately.

Root and shoot tissues were oven-dried for analysis. DCB plaque extraction begins with fresh roots; its concentration denominator is not expressly defined and remains basis-not-reported.
sources.methods: Rice grown under controlled conditions, iron plaque induced by an 80 mg/L ferrous treatment for 24 h and exposed to a 1 mg/L CrCl 3·6 H 2 O-labelled treatment for 3 days. Nominal salt-versus-element wording is retained as a method ambiguity. DCB plaque extraction; dried tissues nitric-acid digested and analyzed by ICP-OES with blanks/reference material. µ-XRF, µ-XANES and 13 C NanoSIMS support spatial/speciation interpretation; a 16-day dissolution experiment samples days 1, 3, 7, 10, 16.
sources.implications: Supports chromium uptake and iron-plaque pathway evidence. Hotspot spectral fractions are not bulk rice-grain species fractions and cannot substitute for a Cr(VI) food result. Release of plaque-bound Cr during dissolution qualifies any assumption of permanent sequestration.
sources.fitness: EF-2 for controlled tissue concentrations and hotspot speciation; pathway context only for consumer products. Source-reported distribution calculations require qualification.
sources.notes: HAL cover establishes final title, journal, year and DOI; manuscript title differs slightly. The 87-page bundle repeats manuscript text: counted once. Novel experimental-rice-tissue and iron-plaque matrices exclude food-occurrence admission. Table 1 says mean±SE whereas general Methods says SD; table-specific SE governs. Table 1 distribution percentages are retained as reported and do not consistently equal fractions of its concentrations. Figure 4 c governs spot-specific values. Supporting-information DOCX is a link placeholder on p 85, not embedded data; unlabeled Figure 1/6 bars are not assigned invented exact values.

sources.title: Analysis of a Wild Leafy Vegetable (Premna latifolia Roxb.) Samples for Essential Trace Elements using ICP - MS Technique
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/HPLC-ICP-MS Root-vegetable purées/10-70729-se24205180530.pdf
sources.publication: International Journal of Scientific Engineering and Research 12(2):1–4
sources.sample_population: Premna latifolia leaves from three villages in Kaviti Mandal, Srikakulam, Andhra Pradesh; collection year and independent sample N not reported.
sources.intro: Premna latifolia leaves collected in three Andhra Pradesh villages had different reported elemental concentrations. Village-specific values are preserved as local leafy-vegetable evidence; the paper supplies no replicate counts or uncertainty estimates.
sources.methods: Leaves collected directly from fields, washed twice with distilled water, shade-dried, then 0.5 g digested with nitric acid and hydrogen peroxide. Digests made to 50 mL and analyzed by ICP-MS. No LOD, recovery, reference material or dispersion is reported. Leaf dry-material basis follows sample preparation; no fresh-weight conversion is supplied.
sources.implications: Supports geographic variation in six elements in a specific wild edible leaf. It does not establish nutritional adequacy, safety, or a regional market distribution. The source’s characterization of aluminium as an essential nutrient is not adopted.
sources.fitness: EF-2 for village-level occurrence values with limited sampling and QA metadata. Regional/sample and basis qualifiers must accompany any later reuse.
sources.notes: The PDF footer establishes February 2024, volume 12(2), and paperID SE 24205180530. DOI is absent from the PDF; the manifest DOI was independently matched to the same title/byline/year through Crossref on 2026-09-10 (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.70729/se24205180530). First-author family name Narayana Murthy follows the publisher-deposited Crossref record. Existing broad leafy-vegetables ingredient retains species identity in the groups; no nutrient/safety claim inferred.

sources.title: Bioaccumulation Potential And Speciation Of Arsenic Ions In Vigna Radiate Root Biomass Using Microwave Assisted Extraction By HPLC-ICP-MS
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/HPLC-ICP-MS Root-vegetable purées/10-32622-ijrat-732019166.pdf
sources.publication: International Journal of Research in Advent Technology 7(3):1528–1534
sources.sample_population: Controlled Vigna radiata root-biomass experiment with0,3,5,10mg/L arsenite, three replicates; observations at7,14,21,28days.
sources.intro: An arsenite-exposure experiment measured arsenic species in Vigna root biomass and compared extraction methods. The source’s analytical extraction yield must be distinguished from removal of arsenic from environmental water; no edible seed or market-food measurement is reported.
sources.methods: Odisha-sourced seeds grown in modified Hoagland solution pH 6.8, randomized three-replicate experiment. Root biomass extracted with microwave-assisted procedures, arsenic measured by ICP-MS and species separated using Hamilton PRP-X 100 anion-exchange HPLC; SEM-EDX/FTIR used for material characterization. The paper describes differing extraction temperatures/times, and potentially species-altering digestion/reduction steps without a complete species-recovery validation.
sources.implications: Provides qualified root-speciation and analytical-method context for phytoremediation research. As(III), As(V), MMA and DMA stay separate. It does not demonstrate safe edible legumes or establish 85.14% water remediation.
sources.fitness: EF-3 for qualified experimental/speciation context; extraction conditions, denominator and species-preservation validation are unresolved. Preserve all reported time-point means and SDs.
sources.notes:
The PDF title spells the plant “Vigna radiate”; botanical normalization to Vigna radiata in context is not a new crop finding. DOI is not printed in the preserved PDF; Crossref independently matches title, author and 2019 publication (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.32622/ijrat.732019166). PDF issue says March; Crossref publication date April 10. Table 1 SD governs over Methods SEM. Abstract/conclusion 30°C 30 min conflicts with Methods 40/60/80°C 5/15/25 min and Results 60°C optimum. No exact Figure 1 values are invented. Novel experimental-root-biomass matrix excludes market occurrence; hypothetical bacterial enzyme diagram is not a primary microbiome experiment.

Table 1 uses MAA for methylarsonic acid while the body uses MMA; the structured MMA label retains this author-assigned compound. The DMA table heading says dimethylarsonic acid while the text says dimethylarsinic acid; the source nomenclature conflict is retained.

sources.intro: This Sri Lankan study compares elemental concentrations and simulated digestive release in two leafy vegetables across five growing areas. Raw, coconut-milk-cooked and coconut-oil-stir-fried portions were tested separately; lower in-vitro release does not establish lower human absorption or safe consumption.

Every gastric/intestinal concentration, percentage, dispersion and ND cell from Tables 1–2 is retained in the structured batch table. Overall gastric/intestinal bioaccessibility reported on p 8: Ni 9.98/3.51%, Cd 9.46/5.81%, Cr 3.93/1.97%, Pb 9.70/3.15%, Cu 13.8/33.6%; pooled denominators are not explicit.
sources.methods: 80 samples across Piliyandala, Wellampitiya, Kolonnawa, Kottawa, Bandaragama. Each edible sample split into 200 g portions: raw; 50 mL coconut milk cooking; 15 mL coconut oil stir-frying, 12 minutes at 95±2°C. PBET at 37°C uses gastricpH 2.5 for 1 h and intestinalpH 7 for 2 h. ICP-OES; total analysis by AOAC 999.11 dry ashing. SpinachCRM recovery 96–104%; LODµg/g: Ni 0.025, Cd 0.005, Cr 0.010, Pb 0.050, Cu 0.015. Reported concentration moisture basis is not explicit.
sources.implications: Supports region-specific leafy-vegetable occurrence and cooking/bioaccessibility comparisons. Processing effects are not uniform: for example Wellampitiya A. sessilis gastric Pb is 15.3% raw and 20.7% cooked. Coconut additions can change the matrix; an in-vitro endpoint is not in-vivo absorption.
sources.fitness: EF-2 for source concentrations and region/treatment comparisons; EF-3 for modeled digestive exposure. Keep total plant results separate from digest fractions and preserve nondetection.
sources.notes: Novel in-vitro-digest matrix represents PBET extracts, never a product concentration row. All 50 table rows and their 13 cells are preserved, with source ± treated as unspecified dispersion rather than inventing SD. Tables govern over prose ranges that occasionally disagree. Cr is elemental/unspeciated. WHO/FAO comparisons in table footers are not primary legal evidence. Duplicate/overlapping PDF text layers are counted once; no exact values invented for unlabeled Figure 3/4 bars.

sources.subject: Root-vegetable purées
sources.title: HEAVY METALS ACCUMULATION IN SOIL AND CELERY ROOT (APIUM GRAVEOLENS L.) HARVESTED FROM THE POLLUTED AREAS IN SIBIU COUNTY, CENTRAL ROMANIA
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/Root-vegetable purées bioaccessibility heavy metals/10-52846-aamc-v52i1-1370.pdf
sources.sample_population: Paired soil and celery-root collections from26households in seven Copsa Mica-area settlements,SibiuCounty,2021–2022.
sources.intro: Celery roots and garden soils from 26 households in a historically polluted Romanian area showed wide cadmium and lead variation in 2021–2022. Soil results use dry weight, while edible celeriac results use fresh weight; these paired measurements preserve a legacy-contamination pathway without assigning sole liability to any facility.
sources.key_numbers:
| Matrix | Metal | Min | Max | Median | Geometric mean | Mean | SD | CV% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| soil | Cd | 0.1 | 14.8 | 4.45 | 1.82 | 4.31 | 3.95 | 91.6 |
| soil | Pb | 28 | 326 | 118.5 | 100.9 | 131.2 | 92.5 | 70.5 |
| soil | Zn | 117 | 1076 | 317 | 323.5 | 383 | 238.2 | 62.2 |
| soil | Cu | 25 | 163 | 58.5 | 58.8 | 65.3 | 31.4 | 48.1 |
| root-tuber-vegetables | Cd | 0.058 | 1.254 | 0.311 | 0.362 | 0.463 | 0.321 | 69.3 |
| root-tuber-vegetables | Pb | 0.022 | 0.62 | 0.105 | 0.117 | 0.163 | 0.138 | 84.7 |
| root-tuber-vegetables | Zn | 3.1 | 11.7 | 6.95 | 6.72 | 7.03 | 2.06 | 29.3 |
| root-tuber-vegetables | Cu | 0.6 | 2.51 | 1.41 | 1.27 | 1.35 | 0.45 | 33.3 |

All concentration statistics aremg/kg: soilDW, celeryrootFW. Highest labelled celeryCd 1.254 mg/kgFW at MicăsasaMS 16; highestPb 0.620 at AxenteSeverAS 13. Household-labelled points and source soil/root regression coefficients are retained in structured evidence.
sources.methods: 2021–2022 paired household soil 0–20 cm and celeryroot samples. Soil air-dried and aqua-regia microwave digested; roots tap-water washed twice, chopped, frozen and nitric-acid microwave digested. Flame/graphite-furnace AAS. n 26; source explicitly labels soilDW and celeryFW. Collection includes AxenteSever, Agârbiciu, Bazna, CopșaMică, Micăsasa,Șoala, Târnava.
sources.implications: Supports historical industrial-burden and present edible-root occurrence evidence. Celery here is celeriac, not stalk celery; product routing is root/tuber vegetables. Geographic sampling is targeted to a polluted area and is not a national market sample.
sources.fitness: EF-2 for paired soil/food summary statistics and labelled household measurements. Preserve all summary types and unequal matrix bases; no cross-market pooling assumption.
sources.notes: Novel root-vegetables matrix denotes celeriac. Table 1 Pbmean 131.2 governs over prose incorrectly calling 383.0 the Pbmean (that is Zn). Figure 1 Cdmaximum 14.80 governs over prose 14.08. Figure 3 Znr 0.656 governs over prose 0.565. Figure 2 governs SO 3/SO 5 Cd labels, which are reversed in one sentence. Named historical industrial attribution is paper context, not an adjudication of exclusive responsibility. DOI is absent from the PDF text; Crossref independently matches the same title and byline (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.52846/aamc.v52i1.1370). Use the printed 2022 issue year; Crossref online publication is 2023-01-04.

sources.subject: Root-vegetable purées
sources.title: Levels of heavy metals concentrations in chocolates from Bwari market Abuja FCT, Nigeria
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/Root-vegetable purées adulteration heavy metals/10-54905-disssi-v9i10-e2ijad3057.pdf
sources.sample_population: Two anonymous chocolate products purchased in Bwari market,Abuja; collection date, formulation and cocoa percentage not stated.
sources.intro: Two anonymous chocolate products from Bwari market contained measurable nickel, iron, copper, chromium and lead. Their reported sample concentrations are preserved independently of inconsistent dispersion, intake means and safety comparisons in the paper.
sources.key_numbers:
| Group | Ni mg/kg | Fe mg/kg | Cu mg/kg | Cr mg/kg | Pb mg/kg |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 1.05 | 7.01 | 5 | 3.5 | 0.2 |
| B | 0.91 | 5.95 | 5.02 | 4.66 | 0.29 |
| reported mean | 0.98 | 6.48 | 5.01 | 4.08 | 0.24 |
| reported dispersion | 0.05 | 0.37 | 0.03 | 0.41 | 0.12 |

All 30 source daily-intake estimates from Table 2 are preserved as unvalidated model outputs. The table’s mean rows do not equal the arithmetic mean of its two sample rows.
sources.methods: 0.2 g chocolate microwave-digested using 2 mL 1: 1 nitric acid/hydrogen peroxide, diluted to 10 mL and measured by flame AAS. Blanks/calibration described; no numeric LOD, recovery or replicate count. Intake scenarios use 20 g/day and 20 kg child, 100 g/day and 70 kg adult. Chocolate composition remains unspecified.
sources.implications: Provides a small local occurrence observation with anonymous products. It cannot establish market prevalence, source attribution, or a no-risk conclusion. Total Cr is not Cr(VI).
sources.fitness: EF-2 for individual product concentrations; EF-X for unreconciled intake means and unsupported blanket safety claims. Mean/dispersion values remain explicitly source-reported.
sources.notes:
Table 3 displays Cu 2.00 andCr 0.11 mg/kg comparators below observed means, contradicting the conclusion that every metal is below its comparator. The discussion also changesCu units. Comparators are not verified WHO instruments and are not entered as legal limits. No brands are exposed. SourcePbmean 0.24 anddispersion 0.12 are retained without silently recalculating. Existing broad chocolate route is used; no dark/milk/cocoa-percentage subgroup inferred.

Table 3 secondary comparator findings and unverified WHO-labelled numbers are retained in the batch context dispositions, without being counted as new primary measurements.

sources.subject: Root-vegetable purées
sources.title: Assessment of the Risk of Heavy Metals Accumulation in Vegetable Crops
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/Meta-analysis Root-vegetable purées heavy metals/10-32686-1812-5220-2021-18-4-48-65.pdf
sources.sample_population: Narrative risk-method review with secondary case studies near Dabaoshan,China,and Tomsk,Russia; no new primary sampling population.
sources.intro: Bashkin and Galiulina review vegetable-associated metal exposure assessment and microbial/agronomic risk-management approaches. Chinese and Russian case-study values are secondary reports; they remain traceable to the cited studies and are not counted as new independent occurrence samples.
sources.key_numbers:
Dabaoshan-region estimated dietary intakes,µg/day (review Table 3):

| Site | Food | Cu | Zn | Pb | Cd |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ZX | rice | 1977 | 11693 | 516 | 229 |
| ZX | vegetables | 327 | 2357 | 47 | 59 |
| ZX | reported total | 2304 | 14050 | 563 | 287 |
| FD | rice | 1961 | 9447 | 371 | 406 |
| FD | vegetables | 290 | 3344 | 45 | 53 |
| FD | reported total | 2251 | 12791 | 416 | 459 |
| LQ | rice | 2322 | 11172 | 476 | 269 |
| LQ | vegetables | 339 | 2104 | 39 | 27 |
| LQ | reported total | 2661 | 13276 | 514 | 296 |
| SB | rice | 1721 | 11127 | 425 | 170 |
| SB | vegetables | 352 | 2559 | 49 | 57 |
| SB | reported total | 2073 | 13685 | 474 | 226 |

Tomsk Table 4 preserves 31 crop/metal mean, min, max and dose rows in structured context; Table 5 preserves 11 dose/reference-dose/HQ triplets. Reported combined non-cancer hazard index 1.745 is a historical source-model result.
sources.methods: Narrative synthesis of hazard identification, exposure, dose-response, risk characterization and management. Dabaoshan Tables 3/Figure 1 derive from refs 27–28; Tomsk Tables 4–5/Figure 2 derive from ref 46. Discusses Monte Carlo uncertainty modeling and rhizosphere bacteria that may immobilize metals or alter uptake. No new sampling or systematic review search protocol is described.
sources.implications: Supports exposure-method and remediation literature discovery. Bacterial effects can increase as well as decrease uptake depending on organism, metal and plant; the review does not establish a universal inoculant intervention. Secondary model outputs are not contemporary health or certification thresholds.
sources.fitness: EF-3 for narrative/secondary evidence and EF-X for internally impossible Table 4 summary combinations until original studies resolve them. Preserve provenance without double-counting source datasets.
sources.notes:
Novel literature-exposure-model and secondary-vegetable-summary matrices separate review quotations from independent food data. Table 4 potato Ba mean 0.7 exceeds max 0.2; beet/carrotCu mean 0.3 is below min 1.69 and max 1.4; cabbage Hg mean 8e-5 exceeds max 1.75e-5. These contradictions are source errors, not repaired by inference. Historical reference-dose/limit tables are secondary context, never verified regulations. Table 3 totals occasionally differ from their component sums. Primary contribution is risk-method synthesis with microbial mitigation discussion, not a new metal–microbiome experiment.

Strontium is preserved in the structured context records but has no dedicated metal page; the source and soil-to-plant hub retain that route gap. Historical comparator columns and Figure 2 are explicitly recorded as secondary context dispositions.

sources.subject: Root-vegetable purées
sources.title: Application of principal component analysis in the pollution assessment with heavy metals of vegetable food chain in the old mining areas
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/Meta-analysis Root-vegetable purées heavy metals/1752-153X-6-156.pdf
sources.sample_population: Three Banat areas: Ruschita,MoldovaNoua and Borlova reference;27soil composites from10grabs each;27vegetable/tissue-region summaries reused from Harmanescu2011.
sources.intro: Gergen and Harmanescu analyze metal contamination patterns across two historic Romanian mining areas and a reference area. Their PCA study reproduces vegetable concentrations and male hazard quotients from the earlier Harmanescu 2011 study; these remain linked secondary observations rather than additional independent samples.
sources.methods: Subsistence farms in Ruschita and Moldova Noua mining areas and Borlova reference. Nine soil composites per area, each 10 grabs, 0–20 cm. Soil aqua-regia extraction; plant ash at 550°C 8 h dissolved in 0.5 N nitric acid. FAAS, certified reference materials; recoveries 92–105%, variation coefficients<10%. PCA on logged values using PAST. Detailed sampling and vegetable data refer to prior study 61; the preserved paper does not give collection dates.
sources.implications: Supports legacy mining and tissue/region differences. Parsley root and leaf remain distinct, as do carrot root and leaf. The fresh-matter food table is retained with cohort linkage so that a reanalysis cannot inflate the evidence pool. Source THQ rankings are model results, not clinical outcomes.
sources.fitness: EF-2 for qualified region/tissue summaries and soil measurements; EF-3 for secondary hazard models. Prior-cohort duplication, LOD context and missing dates must be resolved for pooling.
sources.notes: Broad vegetables matrix is a vocabulary extension; structured rows specify tissue. Table 3 explicitly identifies secondary 2011 data; Table 4 also says compiled from 2011. Several rounded vegetable entries are below the paper’s listed analyticalLOD; retain printed values with qualification. No source safety ranking is adopted. SupplementaryPCA plots are referenced but not embedded; source plot loadings are model context, not additional food measurements.

sources.title: Mercury Contamination of Water and the Removal of Mercury from Water
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/mercury contamination Root-vegetable purées/10-54097-hset-v26i-4008.pdf
sources.sample_population: Narrative review of mercury emission pathways and removal materials; no new samples.
sources.intro: Wen reviews historical mercury releases from combustion, mining and natural exchange, then discusses adsorption and carbon-dot-modified chitosan fabrics. The review is useful for discovery and pathway context but contains chemical and numerical errors that preclude treating its broad safety or efficacy statements as verified findings.
sources.key_numbers:
Secondary estimates include Guizhou anthropogenic emissions 22.6–55.5 source-reported tons/year around 2000, reported as 6.3–10.3% ofChina’s total; Guizhou coal emissions<5 source-reported tons in 1981 andapproximately 26 source-reported tons in 2006; CaliforniaHg production 220 million pounds over 1850–1981. These are review quotations, not current inventories.

Reported coal-emission fractions Hg(0)56%, Hg(II)33%, particulateHg 13% sum 102%. The review describes five fabric reuse cycles without tabulated quantitative removal capacity.
sources.methods: Narrative review of published emission inventories and adsorption studies. No systematic search protocol, new analytical method or independent environmental sampling. Distinguishes historical geographies and time spans; source references remain required for primary verification.
sources.implications: Supports mercury source-pathway and removal-material discovery. Claims that mercury compounds are generally harmless or that only elemental mercury is toxic are rejected; the paper itself contradicts them in its introduction. No current emissions trend or safe discharge concentration is inferred.
sources.fitness: EF-3 for qualified historical/pathway discovery; EF-X for the erroneous chemical generalizations and unvalidated quantitative efficacy claims.
sources.notes:
Novel secondary-environmental-evidence matrix keeps review estimates outside occurrence pools. DOI absent from preserved PDF text was independently matched through Crossref (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.54097/hset.v26i.4008). Historical production is not an environmental emission mass. A blanketUS 10 ppbdischarge claim is unverified secondary context and is not a regulatory-register entry. Figure 1 unlabelledyear values are not interpolated.

The carbon-dot/chitosan claim has an analyte mismatch: cited reference 19 concerns Cr(VI) detection and adsorption, not mercury. The five-cycle statement is therefore EF-X for Hg and is retained only as a citation-error trace. Source “tons” is preserved without assuming metric or US short tons.

sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/Root-vegetable purées mitigation heavy metals/56267.pdf
sources.sample_population: LaboratoryE.coli/S.aureuscultures and aquaticEichhornia/Pistiaplants; treatment2–10ppmNi/Co; replication not specified.
sources.intro: This experiment compares bacterial cultures and aquatic plants under nickel and cobalt exposure. Its charts and narrative describe remediation potential, but missing residual concentrations, uncertainty and method details prevent a reproducible quantitative removal estimate.
sources.key_numbers: Nominal nickel and cobalt treatments: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 ppm. PlantAAScharts compare day 1 withday 20. Bacterial colorimetry is plotted across 0–4 hours forE. coli and 0–2 hours forS. aureus. No exact residual or percentage-removal data are tabulated, so nominal dose is retained separately from outcome.
sources.methods: Cultures sourced from a Kalyan college; aquatic plants collected from the Besol River, Nalambi Gaon, Ambernath, Maharashtra. PreparedNi/Costock dilutions and nutrient broth; plant endpointAAS and bacterial colorimetry. The paper supplies no calibration curve for converting bacterial optical response to dissolved metal, no sampling denominator, and no statistical uncertainty.
sources.implications: Supports bounded remediation-method context. Colorimetric bacterial growth cannot by itself establish metal removal; the claim of superior plant performance is not a validated paired efficacy estimate. Pure bacterial isolates do not measure a host microbiome.
sources.fitness: EF-3 for experimental design and qualitative observations; EF-X for quantitative efficacy claims until residual-concentration and control data are available.
sources.notes: Novel experimental-remediation-water and bacterial-culture matrices prevent food occurrence routing. Abstract and discussion differ in how effective bacteria are described; preserve that limitation. No plant-species-by-metal efficacy matrix is invented from ambiguous chart legends. DOI independently matched via Crossref because absent fromPDF text (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.36948/ijfmr.2025.v07i05.56267); PDF spells coauthor Shreshta, Crossref Shreshtha; retain PDF byline. Microbial remediation is routed as environmental context, not evidence of human gut effects.

sources.title: Oxidative stress in stingless bees exposed to pesticides and heavy metals: a systematic review
sources.file: Systematic review Root-vegetable purées heavy metals/10-36560-19320262200.pdf
sources.source_path: raw/Research Pull HMI/Root-vegetable purées/Systematic review Root-vegetable purées heavy metals/10-36560-19320262200.pdf
sources.sample_population: Qualitative systematic review of18stingless-bee studies,predominantlyBrazil; only one listed copper-sulfate study,no new bee samples.
sources.intro: This review synthesizes oxidative-stress and physiological responses to pesticides and heavy metals in stingless bees. Its copper-sulfate evidence concerns laboratory bee exposure and pollinator health; it supplies no honey concentration or human exposure measurement.
sources.key_numbers: 18 studies included. The copper-sulfate row (Bernardes 2022) lists five oral-exposure concentrations: 5000, 1666.7, 554.2, 183.4, 58.4µg/mL **CuSO4**, not elementalCu. No numericLC 50 or antioxidant-effect magnitude is reproduced for that study.
sources.methods: Web of Science and Scopus searches via CAPES, duplicate removal and title/abstract/full-text screening. Included empirical Meliponini studies assessing contaminant exposure and oxidative-stress biomarkers; qualitative synthesis rather than pooled effect-size analysis. Search dates and full reproducible search strings are not supplied.
sources.implications: Supports pollinator ecotoxicology and metal/pesticide stress-pathway context. Reported copper effects include mortality, locomotion, midgut damage and oxidative/apoptotic responses; do not extrapolate these endpoints to human health or honey contamination.
sources.fitness: EF-3 for qualitative secondary ecotoxicology and source discovery. Retrieve the cited copper study before species-specific quantitative interpretation.
sources.notes: Novel bee-laboratory-diet and ecotoxicology-review matrices prevent food occurrence admission. Table 1 and the Bernardes reference identifyPartamona helleri, whilep 7 misattributes copper findings toScaptotrigona bipunctata. Table/reference identity governs and the conflict remains flagged. Copper sulfate formulation doses are never converted to elementalCu without salt details. Pesticide-only studies are coexposure context, not heavy-metal observations; digestive-tissue injury is not a microbiome measurement.

observations.note: Compound dose,not elementalCu; no salt hydration or conversion assumed.

product_context_dispositions.reason: Experimental metal-spiked and NPK-treated crop plots; all 47 concentration/yield/context observations retained as experimental-crop or soil. Crop-specific mitigation evidence is visible; no market occurrence distribution inferred.

Plant dry ashing at 450°C, nitric/hydrochloric acid dissolution and AAS; preparation does not establish the reporting moisture basis.
